stem: Approximately what percentage of clean, dry air is nitrogen?

options.rationale: This is the percentage of oxygen.
Argon makes up just under 1%.
Nitrogen is the main gas in air.
This is roughly the percentage of carbon dioxide.

explanation: Clean, dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide by volume.

stem: Which method is used to separate liquid air into nitrogen, argon and oxygen?

options.content: filtration
options.rationale: Filtration separates solids from liquids; it is only used to remove dust at the start.

options.content: chromatography
options.rationale: Chromatography separates dissolved substances, such as dyes.

options.content: electrolysis
options.rationale: Air is not an electrolyte.

options.content: fractional distillation
options.rationale: The gases have different boiling points.

explanation: Liquid air is a mixture of liquids with different boiling points, so it is separated by fractional distillation.

stem: True or false: air is a mixture, not a compound.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: its gases are not chemically combined, its composition varies a little, and it can be separated by physical means.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. The gases in air are simply mixed, which is why fractional distillation can separate them.

explanation: Air is a mixture of elements (nitrogen, oxygen, argon) and compounds (carbon dioxide, water vapour). They can be separated physically because they have different boiling points.

stem: Nitrogen boils at −196 °C, argon at −186 °C and oxygen at −183 °C. Which gas collects as a **liquid at the bottom** of the fractionating column?

options.content: nitrogen
options.rationale: Nitrogen has the lowest boiling point, so it leaves from the top as a gas.

options.content: oxygen
options.rationale: It has the highest boiling point, so it stays liquid longest.

options.content: argon
options.rationale: Argon is drawn off part-way up the column.

options.content: carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is removed before the air is liquefied.

explanation: The highest boiling point is the least negative: −183 °C for oxygen. Oxygen is the last to boil, so it collects as a liquid at the bottom of the column.

stem: Welders burn ethyne (acetylene) in a gas obtained from the fractional distillation of liquid air to produce a very hot flame. Name the gas.

rejected.feedback: Argon is used to shield welds, not to burn the fuel.

explanation: An oxy-ethyne (oxy-acetylene) torch burns ethyne in pure oxygen, giving a flame hot enough to cut and weld steel.

stem: Why are carbon dioxide and water vapour removed from air before it is liquefied?

options.content: They are poisonous to the workers.
options.rationale: This is not the reason for removing them.

options.content: They would react with the liquid nitrogen.
options.rationale: Nitrogen does not react with them.

options.content: They would explode when compressed.
options.rationale: They do not explode.

options.content: They would freeze into solids and block the pipes.
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide and water become solid long before −200 °C.

explanation: Water freezes at 0 °C and carbon dioxide becomes solid at −78 °C. At the very low temperatures needed to liquefy air they would form solids that block the equipment.

stem: Which gas is drawn off **part-way up** the fractionating column, between the other two main fractions? (Boiling points: N₂ −196 °C, Ar −186 °C, O₂ −183 °C)

options.content: argon
options.rationale: Its boiling point lies between those of nitrogen and oxygen.

options.content: nitrogen
options.rationale: Nitrogen leaves from the top of the column.

options.content: oxygen
options.rationale: Oxygen collects as a liquid at the bottom.

options.content: helium
options.rationale: Helium does not liquefy at these temperatures; it stays with the nitrogen gas.

explanation: Argon boils at −186 °C, between nitrogen (−196 °C) and oxygen (−183 °C), so it is collected part-way up the column.
hints: Put the boiling points in order.

stem: Cattle breeders store frozen bull semen in flasks of liquid nitrogen. Why is liquid nitrogen suitable?

options.content: It supplies oxygen to keep the cells alive.
options.rationale: Nitrogen does not supply oxygen.

options.content: It is very cold (−196 °C) and unreactive, so cells stay frozen safely.
options.rationale: Very low temperature and lack of reactivity are both needed.

options.content: It is a strong acid that kills any bacteria present in the semen.
options.rationale: Liquid nitrogen is not an acid.

options.content: It slowly warms the cells to body temperature.
options.rationale: It keeps them frozen, not warm.

explanation: Liquid nitrogen boils at −196 °C, so it keeps samples deeply frozen for years, and nitrogen is very unreactive, so it does not damage them.
hints: What is the boiling point of nitrogen?

stem: Air contains 21% oxygen by volume. Calculate the volume of oxygen in 250 dm³ of air.
Select **all** the uses of nitrogen.

options.content: making ammonia in the Haber process
options.rationale: Nitrogen is a raw material for ammonia.

options.content: filling packets of crisps to stop them going stale
options.rationale: Unreactive nitrogen keeps oxygen away from the food.

options.content: burning with ethyne in welding torches
options.rationale: This uses oxygen.

options.content: freezing and storing food or biological samples (as liquid nitrogen)
options.rationale: Liquid nitrogen is extremely cold.

options.content: filling party balloons so that they float
options.rationale: Helium is used for this.

options.content: helping patients who cannot breathe properly
options.rationale: Patients are given oxygen.

explanation: Nitrogen is used to make ammonia, as an unreactive gas in food packaging and, as a liquid, for freezing. Oxygen is used in welding and medicine; helium fills balloons.
hints: Think about nitrogen's lack of reactivity and its very low boiling point.

stem: Complete the sentences about the fractional distillation of liquid air.

payload.template: The gas with the lowest boiling point is {{blank:a}}. It leaves from the {{blank:b}} of the column. Oxygen collects as a liquid at the {{blank:c}} of the column.

explanation: Nitrogen (−196 °C) boils most easily and rises to the top; oxygen (−183 °C) has the highest boiling point and stays as a liquid at the bottom.

stem: Match each gas to one of its uses.

right.content: shielding gas in welding and filling light bulbs

explanation: Oxygen supports breathing; argon is unreactive; neon glows when electricity passes through it; carbon dioxide does not support burning and is denser than air. Making ammonia uses nitrogen.
hints: One use belongs to nitrogen, which is not in the list.

stem: An air-separation plant produces liquid oxygen and liquid nitrogen.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Why is the air first passed through filters?

options.content: to remove nitrogen
options.rationale: Nitrogen is a product, not an impurity.

options.content: to remove dust
options.rationale: Dust would contaminate the products and damage the equipment.

options.content: to warm it up
options.rationale: Filters do not warm the air.

options.content: to remove argon
options.rationale: Argon is separated later, in the column.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why carbon dioxide and water vapour must be removed before the air is cooled.

points.description: They would turn into solids (ice and solid carbon dioxide) at the low temperatures
The solids would block the pipes/equipment

parts.explanation: Water freezes at 0 °C and carbon dioxide turns solid at −78 °C. Long before the air reaches −200 °C they would become solid ice and dry ice, which would block the pipes and valves.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The compressed air is allowed to expand through a narrow valve. What happens to its temperature?

options.content: It rises.
options.rationale: Compressing a gas warms it; expanding cools it.

options.content: It stays the same.
options.rationale: Expansion through the valve cools the gas.

options.content: It rises to the boiling point of water.
options.rationale: The process cools the air, not heats it.

options.content: It falls.
options.rationale: Expanding gas cools; this is used to cool the air until it liquefies.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: To about what temperature must air be cooled to become completely liquid?

options.content: about −200 °C
options.rationale: This is below the boiling point of nitrogen (−196 °C).

options.content: about 0 °C
options.rationale: Only water vapour would condense at 0 °C.

options.content: about −78 °C
options.rationale: Only carbon dioxide would solidify at −78 °C.

options.content: about −100 °C
options.rationale: This is still far above the boiling points of nitrogen and oxygen.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why nitrogen leaves from the top of the fractionating column.

points.description: Nitrogen has the lowest boiling point (−196 °C), so it boils first / stays as a gas and rises

parts.explanation: Nitrogen has the lowest boiling point (−196 °C), so it boils most easily and rises to the top as a gas.

explanation: The air is filtered, then carbon dioxide and water vapour are removed so that they do not freeze and block the pipes. It is compressed, cooled and expanded repeatedly until it liquefies at about −200 °C. In the column, nitrogen (lowest boiling point) leaves at the top.
hints: What happens to water and carbon dioxide at very low temperatures?

stem: A sample of 600 dm³ of clean, dry air is measured at room temperature and pressure. (Air: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen by volume; one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.; Ar: O = 16)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of nitrogen in the sample.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of oxygen in the sample.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount, in moles, of oxygen.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of oxygen in the sample.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Argon makes up less than 1% of air. Suggest why it is still worth collecting.

points.description: It has valuable uses (welding shield gas, filling light bulbs) because it is unreactive / huge volumes of air are processed

parts.explanation: Argon is useful because it is unreactive (for example as a shielding gas in welding and to fill light bulbs), and because a plant processes enormous volumes of air, even 0.9% gives a large amount.

explanation: Nitrogen: 0.78 × 600 = 468 dm³. Oxygen: 0.21 × 600 = 126 dm³ = 126 ÷ 24 = 5.25 mol, with a mass of 5.25 × 32 = 168 g.
hints: Oxygen gas is O₂, so its Mr is 32.

stem:
The table gives the boiling points of some gases found in air.

| Gas | helium | neon | nitrogen | argon | oxygen | krypton | xenon |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Boiling point / °C | −269 | −246 | −196 | −186 | −183 | −153 | −108 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Air is cooled to −200 °C. Which gases in the table do **not** turn into liquids?

options.content: krypton and xenon
options.rationale: Their boiling points are well above −200 °C, so they liquefy.

options.content: nitrogen and oxygen
options.rationale: Both boil above −200 °C, so both are liquids at −200 °C.

options.content: helium and neon
options.rationale: Their boiling points are below −200 °C.

options.content: argon and oxygen
options.rationale: Both liquefy at −200 °C.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: In which part of the fractionating column would krypton and xenon end up?

options.content: in the liquid oxygen at the bottom
options.rationale: Their boiling points are higher than oxygen's.

options.content: in the nitrogen at the top
options.rationale: They boil at much higher temperatures than nitrogen.

options.content: with the argon part-way up
options.rationale: They boil well above argon and oxygen.

options.content: They escape before the air is liquefied.
options.rationale: They liquefy easily because their boiling points are relatively high.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the difference between the boiling points of nitrogen and oxygen, in °C.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why it is much harder to separate argon from oxygen than nitrogen from oxygen.

points.description: Argon and oxygen have very close boiling points (only 3 °C apart)
Fractional distillation separates by boiling point, so a very tall column / many stages are needed (nitrogen and oxygen are 13 °C apart)

parts.explanation: Fractional distillation separates substances by their boiling points. Argon (−186 °C) and oxygen (−183 °C) boil only 3 °C apart, compared with 13 °C between nitrogen and oxygen, so a much taller column with many more stages is needed to separate them.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest why most helium is not obtained from air.

points.description: Air contains only a tiny trace of helium / helium does not liquefy at −200 °C, so it is far cheaper to get it from natural gas

parts.explanation: Air contains only a tiny trace of helium, and helium does not liquefy at the temperature used, so it is far cheaper to extract it from natural gas, which contains much more.

explanation: Gases with boiling points below −200 °C (helium, neon) stay as gases; those with higher boiling points (krypton, xenon) collect with the liquid oxygen. Nitrogen and oxygen are 13 °C apart, but argon and oxygen only 3 °C, so argon is hard to separate from oxygen.
hints: A higher boiling point means a gas condenses more easily.

stem: Why is carbon dioxide used in some fire extinguishers?

options.content: It reacts with the burning fuel and turns it into a non-flammable compound.
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide does not react with fuels.

options.content: It is lighter than air and blows the flames away.
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is denser than air.

options.content: It is denser than air and does not support burning, so it smothers fire.
options.rationale: It keeps oxygen away from the fuel.

options.content: It contains oxygen, which cools the burning fuel.
options.rationale: The oxygen in CO₂ is combined and cannot support burning.

explanation: Carbon dioxide does not burn or support burning, and because it is denser than air it settles over the fire and keeps oxygen out.
hints: Think about density and whether it supports burning.

stem: Describe how oxygen and nitrogen are obtained from the air by liquefaction and fractional distillation. [6]

points.description: Air is filtered to remove dust
Carbon dioxide and water vapour are removed, because they would freeze and block the pipes
The air is compressed (and the heat produced is removed)
It is cooled by expansion, repeatedly, until it liquefies at about −200 °C
Liquid air is fractionally distilled in a column; nitrogen (lowest b.p., −196 °C) leaves at the top as a gas
Oxygen (highest b.p., −183 °C) collects as a liquid at the bottom (argon is drawn off between)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The air is filtered to remove dust. Carbon dioxide and water vapour are then removed, because at the low temperatures used they would freeze and block the pipes. The clean air is compressed, which warms it, and the heat is removed. The compressed air is then allowed to expand, which cools it; repeating this cycle cools the air until it liquefies at about −200 °C. The liquid air is fed into a fractionating column. Nitrogen has the lowest boiling point (−196 °C), so it boils off and leaves from the top of the column as a gas. Argon (−186 °C) is drawn off part-way up, and oxygen, which has the highest boiling point (−183 °C), collects as a liquid at the bottom.

explanation: The process has two parts: liquefying the cleaned air, then separating it by boiling point.
hints: Clean, compress, cool, expand, then distil.

stem: A flask of liquid air is left open in a laboratory. Over time, the remaining liquid becomes richer in oxygen. Why?

options.content: Oxygen from the room air dissolves in the liquid.
options.rationale: Evaporation, not dissolving, is the main process here.

options.content: Nitrogen has a lower boiling point, so it evaporates faster.
options.rationale: The liquid left behind contains a growing proportion of oxygen.

options.content: Nitrogen reacts slowly with the glass of the flask and is removed.
options.rationale: Nitrogen is very unreactive.

options.content: Oxygen is made from the nitrogen as it warms up.
options.rationale: One element cannot turn into another in this way.

explanation: Nitrogen (−196 °C) boils more easily than oxygen (−183 °C), so nitrogen evaporates first. The liquid left becomes richer in oxygen, which is the same idea used in fractional distillation.
hints: Which gas has the lower boiling point?

stem: True or false: most of the carbon dioxide sold for fizzy drinks is obtained by the fractional distillation of liquid air.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: It is false. Carbon dioxide is removed from the air before liquefaction, and air contains only about 0.04% of it. Commercial carbon dioxide is mostly collected from other processes, such as fermentation.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: carbon dioxide is removed before the air is liquefied; commercial supplies come mainly from other processes.

explanation: Air contains only about 0.04% carbon dioxide, and it is removed at the start of the process. Carbon dioxide for sale is collected as a by-product of processes such as fermentation and the manufacture of hydrogen for ammonia.
hints: What happens to carbon dioxide at the start of air separation?

stem: Why is argon blown over the hot metal when some metals are welded?

options.content: Argon burns and makes the welding flame hotter.
options.rationale: Argon does not burn.

options.content: Argon reacts with the hot metal to make the weld stronger and harder.
options.rationale: Argon is unreactive.

options.content: Unreactive argon keeps oxygen away, so the hot metal cannot oxidise.
options.rationale: It acts as a protective shield.

options.content: Argon cools the hot metal quickly after welding.
options.rationale: Its main purpose is to exclude oxygen.

explanation: Argon is a noble gas with a full outer shell, so it is unreactive. It forms a shield around the hot weld so that oxygen in the air cannot react with the metal.
